beats.content: Liskov Substitution Principle says: if code works with a parent class, it should work correctly with any subclass too, no surprises. Not just compiles, but actually behaves correctly.

The classic example is Square extending Rectangle. Geometrically, a square is a rectangle, so the inheritance seems fine. But if you set width to 5 and height to 10 on a Square, both dimensions silently become 10. Code that expected area of 50 gets 100. That's the violation.

candidates miss: LSP is about behavioral substitutability, not just compile-time type compatibility. The code compiles fine with Square in place of Rectangle. It breaks at runtime. That's the distinction interviewers are testing.

question: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle?
title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) explained
direct_answer: **LSP** says that objects of a **subclass** should be replaceable for objects of their **superclass** without breaking the program. If class B extends class A, anywhere you use an A object you should be able to use a B object and get the same correct behavior — no surprises, no exceptions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand LSP in terms of behavioral substitution, not just compile-time type compatibility
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking that if code compiles with a subclass it satisfies LSP — it must also behave correctly

question: How do you fix a Liskov Substitution Principle violation?
title: Fixing LSP violations — composition vs inheritance
direct_answer: The usual fix is to **not use inheritance** where the subclass cannot truly substitute the parent. Instead, use a **common interface** without the problematic shared state, or use **composition**. If Square and Rectangle have incompatible behavior, they should both implement a Shape interface independently rather than one extending the other.

speakable_v2.hook: If your subclass has a method that just throws, you've written an LSP violation and hidden it behind a try-catch.

beats.content: When a subclass overrides a method only to throw UnsupportedOperationException, it's telling you: this class can't actually fulfill the parent's contract. Any caller that uses the parent type will break at runtime when they get the subclass.

The Penguin example makes it concrete. Penguin extends Bird but throws on fly(). A method that iterates birds and calls fly() works fine in tests with just Bird instances, then crashes in production when a Penguin appears.

sharp edge: the Java Collections API has this debate. Collections.unmodifiableList returns a List, but calling add() throws. Technically that's an LSP violation. The practical tradeoff is that the alternative, a separate ReadOnlyList type, would fragment the API. Knowing this real-world tension shows you've thought beyond textbook examples.

speakable_v2.cap: UnsupportedOperationException in a subclass is an LSP smell. The right fix is redesigning the hierarchy, not catching the exception.

question: What does throwing UnsupportedOperationException in a subclass mean for LSP?
title: UnsupportedOperationException and LSP violation
direct_answer: Throwing **UnsupportedOperationException** in a subclass method is an **LSP violation**. It means the subclass cannot fulfill the contract of the parent — code that calls that method on the parent type will **break at runtime** when given the subclass. A real-world example is Collections.unmodifiableList() — calling add() throws, which surprises callers.

sections.content: Throwing UnsupportedOperationException in a subclass is a red flag for LSP. It tells you the subclass cannot fully honor the contract of the parent. If I have a Bird class with a fly method, and Penguin extends Bird but throws on fly, then code that calls fly on a Bird reference will break at runtime when given a Penguin. The fix is to not use that inheritance relationship — maybe Penguin and Bird should both implement an Animal interface, and only flying birds implement a FlyingBird interface.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot app applying SOLID principles
speakable_v2.hook: LSP isn't just about class hierarchies. Every interface implementation is a contract, and contracts can be violated too.

beats.content: When a class implements an interface, it's making a behavioral promise. The interface says: give me X, I'll give you back Y. An implementation that returns null, swallows the call silently, or throws unexpectedly breaks that promise, even if the code compiles perfectly.

A List implementation whose add() does nothing is an LSP violation. Callers expect the item to be there after the call. Getting surprised by an empty list is exactly the kind of behavioral mismatch LSP guards against.

non-obvious: the formal version of this is Design by Contract, where you document preconditions, postconditions, and invariants. In Java you don't always write contracts explicitly, but they exist implicitly in every interface. LSP says every implementation must honor those implicit contracts.

speakable_v2.cap: LSP applies to every interface implementation, not just class inheritance. If callers would be surprised, the contract is broken.

question: How does LSP relate to interface contracts?
title: LSP and interface contracts — behavioral expectations
direct_answer: LSP is really about **honoring contracts**. When a class implements an interface, it **promises** to fulfill that contract. If an implementation silently does nothing, throws unexpectedly, or returns wrong values, it violates the contract — even if it compiles. **Design by Contract** is the formal version of this: preconditions, postconditions, and invariants must be maintained.

sections.title: Contract = expected behavior
sections.content: When you implement an interface, the interface is a contract. It says: if you pass in X, you get back Y. An implementation that takes X and returns null, or throws an unexpected exception, or has a side effect the caller did not expect — all of these violate the contract. LSP says every implementation must honor the full contract, not just satisfy the compiler.

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: LSP is really about honoring behavioral contracts, not just type hierarchies. When a class implements an interface, it is making a promise about how it will behave. If I implement a List interface and my add method does nothing — the code compiles, but callers will be surprised when their items do not appear. That is an LSP violation. Every implementation should behave consistently with what callers expect from the interface.

gotcha: a lot of developers use real-world vocabulary to drive inheritance decisions. That leads to exactly the Square-Rectangle problem. The right question for inheritance is: can this subclass be safely substituted for the parent in all contexts? If yes, inherit. If no, use an interface or composition.

question: What is the difference between is-a and behaves-like-a in inheritance?
title: is-a vs behaves-like-a — LSP in inheritance design
direct_answer: **is-a** is a structural (taxonomy) relationship — a Square is mathematically a Rectangle. **behaves-like-a** is the LSP requirement — a Square must behave exactly like a Rectangle in all the ways callers depend on. In OOP, inheritance should be based on **behavioral substitutability**, not taxonomic classification.

sections.title: Taxonomy vs behavior
sections.content: In real-world taxonomy, a Square IS-A Rectangle. In OOP, that only justifies inheritance if Square can substitute for Rectangle in all behavioral contexts. If the Rectangle contract says setWidth and setHeight are independent, Square cannot honor that. The OOP rule is: use inheritance when the subclass truly behaves like the parent — not just when it fits the parent's real-world category.

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: The is-a relationship is about real-world classification — a square is a rectangle in geometry. But in object-oriented programming, inheritance should be guided by behaves-like-a: can my subclass replace the parent in every situation without breaking anything? A square in code cannot behave exactly like a rectangle because setting its width also changes its height. That is why we say OOP inheritance should follow behavioral substitutability, not real-world taxonomies.
